Many people get married for various reasons.
Some get married to connect wealthy families.
Others marry to escape their family ties.

Dembe
Dear sister,
I am writing to let you know that I will be leaving my wife.
I have tried to calm her down, but she will not listen to reason.
Yesterday she cooked a meal that I found absolutely disgusting.
Eba and soup, with no meat. Can you imagine?
I did the only thing I could think of in the moment.
I threw it in the garbage and asked her to cook me a decent meal.
She screamed at me and said 'No', very emphatically.
I told her that if she doesn't cook me a proper meal, I will walk out.
She thought I was joking.
I walked out of the house and have not returned since.
I write this letter to you from my brother's house.
If she does not cook this meal, I will not return to the house.
I just wanted to let you know, in case you heard the story from somewhere else.
I am a simple man.
I don't ask for much.
I work in the farm all day. All I want is a decent meal from my wife.
If you have any words of wisdom, I am all ears.
- Dembe
Dear sister,
I took the words you sent me to heart.
I have returned to the house.
I explained my position to my wife, and begged her forgiveness.
She accepted, and cooked the most delicious meal I have ever eaten in my life.
Everything is alright now.
Thank you very much for your help.
- Dembe
Dear sister,
Maybe you don't understand the gravity of the situation.
I did not understand the words you sent.
If you cannot help me, I will seek wisdom from someone more capable.
I will not be responding until you send me something I can use.
- Dembe
St. Hildegard von Bingen
O Viridissima Virga

Hail, O greenest branch,
sprung forth in the airy breezes
of the prayers of the saints.

So the time has come
that your sprays have flourished:
hail, hail to you,
because the heat of the sun has exuded from you
like the aroma of balm.

For the beautiful flower sprung from you
which gave all parched perfumes
their aroma.

And they have radiated anew
in their full freshness.

Whence the skies bestowed dew upon the pasture,
and all the earth was made joyful
because her womb
brought forth corn,
and because the birds of the firmament
built their nests in her.

Then there was harvest ready for Man
and a great rejoicing of banqueters,
whence, O sweet Virgin,
no joy is lacking in you.
Eve rejected all these things.
Now let there be praise to the Highest.
St. Andrew Kim Taegon
Andrew Kim Taegon was the first Korean priest and patron saint of Korean clergy. Kim's father was martyred for practicing Christianity, which was highly prohibited in a heavily Confucian Korea.

Kim studied at seminaries at the Portuguese colony of Macau as well as at Lolomboy, Bocaue, Bulacan, Philippines, eventually attaining his ordination as a priest in Shanghai by the French bishop Jean Joseph Jean-Baptiste Ferréol after almost a decade in training.

Kim returned to Korea to preach and evangelize even as many Christians were persecuted. At the age of 25, he was tortured and beheaded near Seoul on the Han River. Pope John Paul II canonized Kim along with 102 other Korean Martyrs on 6 May 1984.

Elizabeth Ann Bayley Seton grew up in the upper class New York society and married a wealthy young man. Tragedy befell her as she lost her father in-law, her husband's business, and finally, her husband to tuberculosis.

Elizabeth's deep concern for the spiritual welfare of her family and friends eventually led her into the Catholic Church, and she, along with two other young women who helped her in her work, began plans for a Sisterhood, establishing the first free Catholic school in America.

Saint Josephine Margaret Bakhita was born around 1869 in the village of Olgossa in the Darfur region of Sudan. Enjoying a happy childhood, she was soon kidnapped by Arab slave traders and forced to walk barefoot over 600 miles to a slave market in El Obeid.

After spending several years in captivity, where she suffered devastating abuse, she was eventually sold to an Italian Vice Consul, eventually making her way to Italy and joining the Canossian Sisters in Venice where she remained for the rest of her life. She was affectionately known as the "little brown sister", or honorably as the "black mother".

The first Danish king to be canonized, Canute ruled for six short years, succeeding his brother Harald III Hen in 1081. He married Adela, the sister of Count Robert of Flanders and went on to build many churches and monasteries.

In 1085, he set his eyes on the throne of England and devised a plan to invade the country. However, the nobles of the court rebelled against him, forcing him to flee to the isle of Funen where he, his brother Benedict, and seventeen companions were slain by rebels.

He was recognized by the Roman Catholic Church as patron saint of Denmark in 1101.

Saint Elizabeth of Hungary was a princess of the Kingdom of Hungary, Landgravine of Thuringia, Germany. Elizabeth was married at the young age of 14 to Ludwig IV of Thuringia, a German nobleman, with whom she had three beautiful children.

Her happiness was short lived however, as tragedy struck her family during a disease outbreak which took the life of her husband. Her spirit unbroken, she continued to help the less fortunate, providing food for the poor and building a hospital for the sick.

Vowing never to remarry despite pressure from relatives, Elizabeth eventually joined the Third Order of St. Francis where she devoted the rest of her life to God and charitable labor. She died at 24 years of age and was canonized in 1235.

The first Roman Catholic bishop of Quebec and the father of the Canadian Church, Blessed François-Xavier de Montmorency-Laval was one of the most influential men of his day.

As bishop, Laval's dream was not only to expand the Catholic Church in New France, but also to train and teach its future leaders, opening the Grand Séminaire in 1663 with the goal of training missionary priests. He also took interest in practical education for craftsmen and farmers, founding a school of arts and crafts at Saint-Joachim. 

In his later years, Laval continued to collaborate with the colony's high religious authorities, until his last days. The city of Laval, Quebec, north of Montreal, is named after him.

Saint Frederick of Hallum was born to a poor widow, later becoming a Premonstratensian priest, founder and first abbot of Mariengaarde Abbey in Friesland in the Netherlands.

He was also the parish priest of Hallum, his birthplace, and founder of Bethlehem Abbey for Premonstratensian canonesses.

He died and was buried at Mariengaarde but in 1614, to save his relics from the Calvinists, they were removed and taken to Bonne-Espérance Abbey near Estinnes in Belgium, where they were reinterred in 1616 or 1617. They were transferred to Leffe Abbey near Dinant in 1938.

Saint Anthony of Saint Ann Galvăo, commonly known in Brazil as Frei (Friar) Galvão, was a Brazilian friar of the Franciscan Order, and one of the best-known religious figures in colonial Brazil. 

At age 16, he became a novice at St. Bonaventure Friary in Vila de Macacu, Rio de Janeiro where he was known for his piety, zeal and exemplary virtues. Galvão was a man of great and intense prayer, and mystic phenomena attributed to him include telepathy, premonition and levitation. He was also known for his healing powers.

He was canonized by Pope Benedict XVI on May 11, 2007, becoming the first Brazilian-born saint.

Saint Dulce of the Poor was a Brazilian Franciscan Sister who was the founder of the Obras Sociais Irmã Dulce. Born to an upper-middle class family, she was deeply affected after a visit to the poor area of the city with her aunt. She then began to care for the homeless and beggars in her neighborhood.

Immediately after graduation at 18, she joined the Missionary Sisters of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God, in Sergipe and shortly after founded the "São Francisco's Workers Union", the first Christian worker's movement in Bahia.

She later founded Obras Sociais Irmã Dulce, one of the most well-known philanthropic organizations in Brazil, and was nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize by Queen Silvia of Sweden. She was canonized in 2019, making her the first Brazilian female saint.

Queen Jadwiga, also known as Hedwig, was the first female monarch of Poland, ascending to the throne at age 13. An exceptional ruler, she brought about the unification of Poland and Lithuania through her marriage to Władysław-Jogaila and preserved the peace with the Teutonic Order. 

She opened schools, churches, and hospitals while restoring old ones to their former glory. She attended Mass everyday, and in accordance with her family's tradition, was especially devoted to the Blessed Virgin Mary. 

Jadwiga often prayed before a large black crucifix hanging in the north aisle of Wawel Cathedral. During one of these prayers, the Christ on the cross is said to have spoken to her. Pope John Paul II canonized Jadwiga in Kraków on 8 June 1997.

John Roberts was born in a small village in north Wales into a family descended from Welsh nobility. Initially baptized as an Anglican, he later converted to Catholicism during his travels in Europe, eventually making his profession as a Benedictan missionary in 1600.

During a tumultuous period in England at the height of the Protestant Reformation, there was great hostility towards Catholic priests, and John Roberts was arrested on several occasions during his time there; saying Mass and providing aid for plague victims.

He was eventually tried and found guilty under the Act forbidding priests to minister in England, and was hanged, drawn, and quartered, at the age of thirty-three. On 25 October 1970, Roberts was canonized by Pope Paul VI.

Brochero was born in Argentina as the fourth of ten children to Ignacio Brochero and Petrona Davila. At age 16, he commenced his studies to become a priest at the College Seminary of Our Lady of Loreto, where he met future president Miguel Ángel Juárez Celman.

Brochero founded a home known as the Houses of Exercises in 1875, and later established a school for girls in 1880. He was known to travel long distances in Argentina on the back of a mule dressed in a sombrero and a poncho to serve the needs of the Christian faith throughout his huge parish. 

He cared for the sick during the cholera epidemic of 1867 and contracted leprosy during his travels, which eventually led to blindness and deafness towards the end of his life.

Balikuddembe was enrolled as a catechumen and baptized in 1882, taking the baptismal name of "Joseph". After the Catholic missionaries, for reasons of security, moved to the southern end of Lake Victoria, Balikuddembe became leader of the Christians.

Now Danieri Mwanga II succeeded to the throne as King, and began to crack down on Christian missionaries and converts in his country, executing the British Anglican bishop James Hannington and his companions on October 29, 1885, despite Balikuddembe's pleas.

Mwanga, viewing Balikuddembe's disapproval as disrespectful, ordered him executed. He was beheaded and his body was thrown onto a pile of burning firewood. St. Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe Parish in Kisoga is named after him.

Kateri was born in the Mohawk village of Ossernenon. She contracted smallpox during an epidemic which scarred her face at a very young age and killed her entire family. She subsequently moved into the care of her uncle who was the chief of a Mohawk clan.

Trouble came when she refused to marry, despite the many attempts by her adoptive parents. She later converted to Catholicism, taking a vow of chastity and pledging to marry only Jesus Christ, a decision that was met with disdain among her adoptive parents and neighbors.

She eventually moved to a Christian native community south of Montreal, where she practiced a very devout lifestyle. She died at the young age of 24. Her name, Kateri, is the Mohawk form of Catherine, which she took from St. Catherine of Siena.

Born in Philadelphia to a prominent and wealthy banker, Katharine Drexel received a solid education from private tutors and traveled throughout the United States and Europe. 

Sometime after receiving spiritual direction from Father James O' Connor, she began her six-month postulancy at the Sisters of Mercy Convent in Pittsburgh in 1889. Shortly after taking her vows, she dedicated her life and fortune to working for the American Indians and African-Americans in the Western United States.

By the time of her death, she had more than 500 Sisters teaching in 63 schools throughout the country and she established 50 missions for Native Americans in 16 different states. She was canonized on October 1, 2000 by Pope John Paul II.

Born around the year 1600 in the Philippines to a Chinese father and a Filipino mother, Lorenzo Ruiz fled the country to Japan after being accused of the murder of a Spaniard.

Unfortunately for him, Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa Shogunate, who were persecuting Christians. Lorenzo and his companions were immediately arrested for being Christians and ordered to recant their faith. On refusal to do so, they were imprisoned for two years.

They were later taken to Nagasaki to be tortured and killed, but Lorenzo and his companions were faithful until the very end. He was canonized at the Vatican on October 18, 1987.

Born in 1611 near Nagasaki, Magdalene was the daughter of a Christian couple who were martyred during the reign of the Tokugawa Shogunate. Magdalene later served as an interpreter for the friars Francis of Jesus Terrero and Vincent of Saint Anthony Simoens and, in 1625, became a tertiary of the Order of Augustinian Recollects.

As the friars were tortured and killed under severe persecution, with many Christians apostatizing, Magdalene turned herself to the authorities, declaring herself a Christian. She was tortured for thirteen days, enduring suffocation, being hung upside down over a pit of offal on a gibbet, and finally, drowning. She died at age 23.

Saint Mariam Thresia, an Indian Syro-Malabar Catholic nun, was the founder of the Congregation of the Holy Family and was best known for her frequent visions and ecstasies, as well as receiving the stigmata.

Throughout much of her life, Thresia received several different spiritual experiences including prophecy, healing, aura of light, frequent ecstasies and levitations. Because of the extreme nature of some diabolical attacks and vexations, Thresia was subjected to several different exorcisms by the Venerable Joseph Vithayathil, under the Bishop's orders.

In 1926, after receiving an injury on her leg which eventually proved to be fatal, St. Mariam Thresia died with her final words being: "Jesus, Mary and Joseph; I give you my heart and my soul."

St. Marguerite D'Youville, born in Quebec, studied under the Ursulines, married Francois D'Youville in 1722, and became a widow in 1730. 

She worked to support herself and her three children, devoting much of her time to the Confraternity of the Holy Family in charitable activities and later founding the Sisters of Charity, the Grey Nuns of Canada.

The Grey Nuns established schools, hospitals and orphanages throughout Canada, the U.S., South America, and Africa and are famous for their work among the Eskimos.

Saint Monica, also known as Monica of Hippo, is the mother of St. Augustine. Born in 331 A.D., Monica was married at a young age to the Roman pagan Patricius and had three children including Augustine. She managed to convert her husband and mother-in-law to Christianity after several years.

Two of her kids entered the religious life, but Augustine cared little for Christianity, so Monica sent him off to Carthage for schooling. To her dismay, Augustine returned a Manichaean, but with great patience, Monica prayed for her son for several years, and with the help of St. Ambrose, Augustine finally converted to the faith.

She was buried at Ostia, and her body was removed during the 6th century to a hidden crypt in the church of Santa Aurea in Osta, near the tomb of St. Aurea of Ostia. The city of Santa Monica in California is named after her.

Moses, an Egyptian government official's slave until his dismissal, was part of a violent gang of robbers until he took shelter with some monks in a colony in the desert of Wadi El Natrun, near Alexandria. 

Moses was so moved by the monks that he gave up his old way of life, became a Christian, was baptized and joined the monastic community at Scetes. He proved to be a prophetic spiritual leader, settling disputes within and outside the community of monks and sometimes carrying a leaking sack of sand on his shoulders to show humility.

After word came of an attack on the monastery by a group of Berbers, Moses ordered the others to leave while staying behind, believing his life had come full circle. He was joined by seven others, and together they were martyred by the bandits around 405 A.D.

Saint Pedro Calungsod, a Filipino Roman Catholic, was a skilled sacristan and teacher of catechism. He accompanied Blessed Diego Luis de San Vitores to the Marianas Islands where many received the sacraments, especially that of baptism.

A plot to have him killed began when a criminal named Choco began spreading false rumors that the baptismal water contained poison. Given that some sickly infants who were baptized eventually died, the story stuck and people began to despise the missionaries.

It came to head when the local chief, who now opposed the missionaries because of the rumors, learned of his newborn daughter's baptism. A violent assault followed, and Pedro, along with San Vitores, were killed in the attack. On October 21, 2012, Pope Benedict XVI canonized Calungsod in Saint Peter's Square.

Roque Gonzalez de Santa Cruz was the son of noble Spanish parents, ordained at twenty-three, and joining the Society of Jesus after a decade of preaching to the Indians of Paraguay in remote regions.

Over the next two decades, Father Roque Gonzalez set up multiple "reductions" - settlements of Christian Indians run by the Jesuit missionaries - grappling with hardships and dangers against fierce tribes and with the opposition of the European colonists.

In 1628, Father Roque Gonzalez met his untimely end when a raiding party, led by a powerful "medicine man", attacked the Mission, killing him and setting the chapel on fire. He was canonized in 1988 by Pope John Paul II.

St. Martin de Porres was born in Lima, Peru. Being of mixed race, he experienced a great deal of ridicule as a young boy. The law in Peru at the time prevented Africans and Native Indians from becoming full members of religious orders, so Martin began as a servant boy at the Dominican Convent of the Rosary.

Martin worked hard and made his way up from church officer to lay brother and finally took his vows as a member of the Third Order of Saint Dominic, granted by the prior who disregarded the racial laws that prohibited his entry. He cared for many people unconditionally, from Spanish nobles to African slaves.

Towards the end of his life, Martin fell very ill with chills, fevers and tremors causing him agonizing pain. He would suffer this illness for almost a year until his eventual death in 1639.

Victor Maurus, a Mauretanian native, was a soldier in the Praetorian guard. A Christian from a very young age, Maurus was sent to the Hippodrome in the presence of the Roman emperor Maximian Herculean to recant his faith.

Refusing to betray his beliefs, Maurus was whipped, imprisoned and, after an almost miraculous escape, imprisoned again. He was then dragged into a nearby elm wood and decapitated around the year 303.

His relics are now part of the Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, built by Ambrose, fourth-century bishop of Milan.
- St. Josephine Bakhita -
- Journey to my true Master -
I remember the sun rising over the vast plains of Darfur, painting the acacia trees in hues of gold and amber.
It was as if the sky itself whispered promises of a gentle day.
This was around the year 1869, though in our village, time flowed not by calendars but by the rhythm of the seasons.
The dry harmattan winds carried stories from distant lands, and the rains turned the earth into a lush cradle for our feet.
I was born into a family of simple farmers.
My parents' faces bore the quiet strength of those who coaxed life from stubborn soil.
My true name, the one they gave me at birth, has faded like a half-remembered dream.
It is lost to the shadows of what came after.
But in those early years, life wove a tapestry of joy.
I chased my brothers and sisters through the fields.
Laughter echoed like birdsong.
The warmth of my mother's hands braided my hair with beads that clicked like tiny bells.
We were poor, yes, but rich in the bonds that held us.
French: When you hear stories of suffering, what do you feel?

English: Stories unfolded by firelight.
Songs wove the stars into our nights.
French: Fearful

English: Let's explore my little village. Here, the well is our gathering place, where the rope creaks, the pots ring, and the morning light dances on the water's surface.
French: Fear is natural and I knew it well, but it can become a prayer.

English: Little did I know that this fragile world would shatter like dry clay under a careless foot.
The day the darkness came, I was no more than seven years old.
French: Sad

English: My limbs still softened with childhood's innocence.
French: Sadness shows the heart is alive and capable of compassion.

English: It was midday.
French: Angry

English: The heat pressed down like a heavy blanket.
French: Anger can be strong but must not rule the heart; I learned this slowly.

English: I had wandered just beyond the village edge to gather firewood.
French: Unsure

English: The air hummed with the buzz of insects.
French: Not knowing how to feel is honest; it is the beginning of understanding.

English: I hummed too, a tune my mother sang to soothe the little ones.
Suddenly, rough hands clamped over my mouth.
They silenced my song.
French: What does freedom mean to you?

English: Raiders, shadowy figures on swift camels with eyes hard as flint, swept me away like a leaf in a storm.
French: To be safe

English: I kicked and screamed, but their grips were iron.
French: Freedom means to have safety and protection in life.

English: The world blurred into a nightmare of dust and terror.
French: To belong

English: They bound me.
French: Freedom can also mean a place where you are accepted and loved.

English: They threw me across a saddle.
French: Tap each word to discover what I felt.

English: They rode hard into the horizon, leaving my village and my family behind forever.
French: Seen: I was no longer invisible.

English: As the sun dipped low, casting long shadows that swallowed the land, I realized this was no game.
French: Safe: No one raised a hand against me.

English: I was taken, stolen from the life I knew.
The name they gave me then was 'Bakhita,' meaning 'fortunate.'
Fortunate? The irony burned like the whip they soon introduced me to.
In their tongue, it was a mocking jest for a child now reduced to property.
The journey to El Obeid unfolded as a descent into hell.
French: Loved: A feeling I had not known before.

English: It was almost... cinematic in its unrelenting brutality, like scenes from an ancient epic where heroes face trials of fire and shadow.
We slaves, children like me, women with haunted eyes, men broken in spirit, were herded like cattle through the scorching sands.
The chains around my ankles chafed raw sores that wept blood.
The guards' whips cracked like thunder.
LatAmSpanish: Fear is natural, but through prayer and trust in God, it can be transformed into courage.

English: They drew crimson lines across our backs.
French: To choose
Filipino: Lifelong service as a Canossian Sister
LatAmSpanish: How do I forgive someone who hurt me?

English: Hunger gnawed at my belly, a constant companion.
French: The greatest part of freedom is being able to make good choices.
LatAmSpanish: Forgiveness is a gift. It does not forget, but it frees your heart to live in peace.

English: We received only scraps that tasted of dirt and despair.
Nights were the worst.
We huddled under threadbare rags.
The stars mocked our captivity with their freedom.
French: I don't know yet
Filipino: Canonization by Pope John Paul II

English: Hyenas howled in the distance.
French: It is okay not to know; freedom is something we grow to understand.
LatAmSpanish: Suffering is part of the human condition, but God is present in our weakness and helps us grow in love.

English: They echoed the cries we stifled to avoid more beatings.
In El Obeid's slave market, the air reeked of sweat, fear, and the metallic tang of blood.
I stood on the auction block.
The sun beat down mercilessly.
Bidders prodded my flesh like merchants inspecting fruit.
My heart pounded like war drums.
I was sold to the highest voice.
Passed from hand to hand, five times, eight times, the numbers blur in memory.
But the pain does not.
Each master marked a new chapter of torment.
My first owner after the raiders was a wealthy merchant.
His home was a sprawling compound of mud-brick walls that trapped the heat like a furnace.
He treated me not as a child but as a beast of burden.
He forced me to carry water from distant wells until my arms screamed in protest.
But it was the second master, a man whose cruelty knew no bounds, who etched his mark upon me forever.
In his household, punishment became an art form.
It was administered with whips, brands, and knives.
They tied me to a tree in the courtyard.
The rough bark bit into my skin.
For some imagined slight, perhaps a spilled drop of water, they scarred me.
Over a hundred times, they say, though I lost count amid the agony.
Hot irons seared patterns into my flesh.
Designs meant to claim ownership became badges of my suffering.
The pain was a white-hot blaze.
It blurred my vision.
It filled my world with screams that were mine and not mine.
Blood pooled at my feet.
It stained the earth red.
As I writhed, the other slaves averted their eyes.
Their silence formed a chorus of shared grief.
Yet even in that inferno, a whisper stirred within me.
It was a mysterious force, like a cool breeze in the desert, sustaining me.
Da schiava non mi sono mai disperata,' I would later say, 'perché sentivo dentro di me una forza misteriosa che mi sosteneva.'
It was God, though I did not know His name then.
He held me when human hands only hurt.
Sold again, to a third master in Khartoum, the capital where the Nile's two arms embraced like old lovers, my life shifted to domestic drudgery.
I cleaned.
I cooked.
I endured the leers of visitors who saw me as exotic curiosities.
The city's bustle offered glimpses of a wider world.
Camels laden with spices plodded through streets.
Merchants haggled in the souks.
The river flowed eternally.
But I remained caged within it.
Then came the fourth sale, to a Turkish general whose temper flared like gunpowder.
His wife, jealous and vicious, wielded the whip herself.
She lashed me for the slightest imperfection in my service.
One night, after a particularly savage beating, I lay on the cool stone floor.
My body was a map of welts and bruises.
I stared at the ceiling's cracks.
They spiderwebbed like my fractured spirit.
The pain throbbed in waves.
But that inner force returned.
It was a quiet assurance that this was not the end of my story.
It was as if an unseen hand traced the scars.
It turned them from marks of shame to something sacred, though I could not yet see it.
Fate, or perhaps Divine Providence, intervened in Khartoum.
I was bought by an Italian consular agent, Callisto Legnani.
His eyes held no malice, only a pragmatic kindness.
For the first time since my abduction, no whip greeted my errors.
In his home, overlooking the Nile's lazy curve where feluccas sailed like white-winged birds, I experienced serenity.
Meals were shared at a table, not scraps from the floor.
Conversations flowed without commands barked in anger.
Yet nostalgia gnawed at me.
The family I lost, the village's songs, they faded like echoes.
Political unrest stirred Egypt and Sudan.
Whispers of uprisings rippled through the city like wind over water.
Signor Legnani decided to flee to Italy.
When he asked if I wished to accompany him and his friend Augusto Michieli, my heart leaped.
Italy? A land across the sea, shrouded in mystery.
I nodded eagerly.
I clung to this thread of hope as we boarded a ship.
It cut through the Mediterranean's azure waves.
The salt spray kissed my face like a promise of renewal.
The voyage was a revelation.
The sea became a vast, undulating canvas under skies that shifted from dawn's pink blush to twilight's violet veil.
We docked in Genoa, Italy's port city alive with the clamor of fishermen and the scent of olive oil and fresh bread.
There, Signora Michieli, with her warm smile and insistent pleas, convinced Signor Legnani to let me stay with their family.
I became part of their world in Zianigo, a quiet village near Venice.
Vineyards stretched like green tapestries.
The air hummed with the peace of rural life.
When little Mimmina was born, a bundle of joy with eyes like polished chestnuts, I was entrusted as her nanny.
Oh, the tenderness of those days!
I rocked her to sleep under canopies of stars.
I sang the lullabies of my lost homeland mixed with Italian melodies.
For the first time, I felt like I belonged.
Mimmina's tiny fingers wrapped around mine.
Her laughter became a balm to my scars.
But even in this idyll, shadows lingered.
The Michielis owned estates in Sudan.
When business called Signora Michieli away, she took Mimmina and left me in Venice with her sister.
She intended my return.
Venice, the city of canals and gondolas gliding like black swans through labyrinthine waterways, bridges arching like lovers' embraces, the air perfumed with sea and stone.
Entrusted to the Canossian Sisters at the Istituto dei Catechumenati, I was to learn Italian and care for the child temporarily left behind.
But God had other plans.
The sisters, daughters of Charity founded by St. Magdalene of Canossa, enveloped me in a love that was gentle and instructive.
It was like sunlight filtering through stained glass.
They taught me not just letters and numbers, but of a Man named Jesus.
He suffered chains and whips yet forgave His tormentors.
As I listened to their stories by the flickering candlelight in the catechism room, with the Grand Canal lapping softly outside, my heart stirred.
This Jesus knew my pain.
His scars mirrored mine, but His were redemptive.
That mysterious force I'd felt in the desert? It had a name: God's love, paternal and unyielding.

Even as a child in Sudan, gazing at the heavens, I had wondered, 'Vedendo il sole, la luna e le stelle, dicevo tra me: Chi è mai il Padrone di queste belle cose? E provavo una voglia grande di vederlo, di conoscerlo e di prestargli omaggio.'
Now, I knew.
He was the Master of all beautiful things.
After a year of preparation, on January 9, 1890, in the Patriarch's cathedral, waters of baptism washed over me.
I emerged as Giuseppina Bakhita.
Confirmed and receiving my First Communion, the Eucharist became a fire in my soul.
Often, I kissed the baptismal font and said, 'Qui sono diventata figlia di Dio!'
I am definitively loved, I felt, and whatever happens to me, I am awaited by this Love.
And so my life is good.
When Signora Michieli returned, demanding I go back to Sudan as her property, the moment unfolded like a dramatic confrontation in a grand opera.
The courtroom in Venice, with its echoing halls and stern judges, became the stage.
She claimed ownership.
But I, empowered by my new faith, refused.
"No," I said, my voice steady though my knees trembled, "I will not leave my Paron, my Master, who is God."
The law sided with me.
Baptism had made me free, a child of Italy and of heaven.
Tears streamed down Signora Michieli's face.
But in her heart, I sensed understanding dawning.
Freed from earthly chains, I chose the heavenly ones.
In 1893, I entered the novitiate of the Canossian Sisters in Verona.
The ancient city's rose-red walls formed a fitting backdrop to my rebirth.
Professing vows on December 8, 1896, in the motherhouse, I surrendered all: poverty, chastity, obedience.
It was not loss, but the ultimate fortune my name foretold.
I called Him 'el me Paron,' my sweet Master.
My life as Sister Giuseppina unfolded in Schio, a modest town in Vicenza's hills.
The sisters ran an institute for orphans, schools, and the needy.
No grand roles awaited me.
God called me to the humble, the hidden.
As cook, I stirred pots over crackling fires.
The steam rose like prayers.
I fed bodies and souls with meals seasoned by charity.
As sacristan, I polished chalices until they gleamed like the sun on the Nile.
I arranged flowers for the altar with hands once scarred, now offering incense of gratitude.
Portress at the gate, I greeted visitors with a smile that masked old pains.
I mended clothes in the evenings by lamplight.
I tended the garden where vegetables grew under my care, like hope in barren soil.
Each task formed a scene in the quiet drama of sanctity.
We woke at dawn for Lauds.
The bells tolled like heartbeats.
Vespers came at dusk.
Shadows lengthened as we sang of God's mercy.
I traveled too, promoting missions across Italy.
My story became a testimony to the Gospel's reach, from Sudanese sands to Venetian spires.
The liberation that I had received through my encounter with the God of Jesus Christ, I felt I had to extend.
It had to be handed on to others, to the greatest possible number of people.
My humility, simplicity, and constant smile conquered the hearts of all in Schio.
My sisters esteemed me for my unalterable sweetness, exquisite goodness, and deep desire to make the Lord known.
Sickness came in my later years.
It was a slow fade like mist over the lagoon.
From 1947, bedridden in Schio's infirmary, pain revisited my body.
But my spirit soared.
Visitors came: children from the institute, sisters with tales of the world.
I regaled them with my life, not as tragedy, but as triumph.
"Be good, love the Lord, pray for those who do us good or harm." I told them.
My voice was a gentle current.
To those who asked how I fared during illness, I replied with a smile, "Come vol el Paron, as the Master wills."
Non è importante quello che sembra tale, ma quello che vuole il Signore.
It is not what seems important, but what the Lord wills.
God's love has always accompanied me in a mysterious way.
The Lord loved me.
You have to love everyone.
You have to have pity.
On February 8, 1947, as snow blanketed the town in white, I slipped away.
In agony, I relived the terrible days of slavery.
I supplicated the nurse who assisted me, 'Mi allarghi le catene... pesano!' Loosen the chains, they weigh!
Maria Santissima freed me from every pain.
My last words were, 'La Madonna! La Madonna!'
While my last smile testified to the encounter with the Mother of the Lord.
At 78, I entered eternity, surrounded by the community in tears and prayer.
A crowd soon poured into the institute's house to see their 'Santa Madre Moretta' one last time and seek her protection from heaven.
Looking back, as if from a director's chair overseeing the reel of my days, I see God's hand in every frame.
From the terror of abduction to the peace of the cloister, He was the unseen producer.
He turned cruelty into conversion.
My story is no mere biography.
It is a call to all who suffer, slaves in body or soul, to grasp that inner force.
Forgive as Christ forgave from the cross.
In Sudan, torn by wars even now, and in every corner where dignity is denied, I intercede.
Pray for peace, for the trafficked, the oppressed.
As Pope John Paul II proclaimed at my canonization in 2000, in St. Peter's Square under a sky vast as Africa's plains, I stand as a shining advocate of genuine emancipation.
The history of my life inspires not passive acceptance but the firm resolve to work effectively to free girls and women from oppression and violence.
To return them to their dignity in the full exercise of their rights.
Pope Benedict XVI reflected on my hope in his encyclical Spe Salvi: "Through the knowledge of this hope she was redeemed, no longer a slave, but a free child of God."
And Pope Francis, in his catechesis, called me "a witness of the transforming power of Christ's forgiveness."
Often a wounded person wounds in turn.
The oppressed easily becomes an oppressor.
Instead, the vocation of the oppressed is that of freeing themselves and their oppressors.
Becoming restorers of humanity.
Only in the weakness of the oppressed can the force of God's love, which frees both, be revealed.
My life, in its arcs of despair and dawn, whispers to you: You are known, loved, awaited.
Live in that hope, and be free.
If I were to meet those slave traders who kidnapped me, and even those who tortured me, I would kneel to kiss their hands.
Because if it had not happened, I would not now be a Christian and religious.
The end.
The village square hums with morning life—women grinding grain, children chasing dust, and the smell of earth warming under the sun.
Uncle's house rests beneath the acacia shade, its cool mud walls and wide doorway always open to family.
Goats bleat and cattle shuffle, their restless movement breaking the quiet as dust swirls around their hooves.
The small schoolyard echoes with bright laughter—a world of chalk, lessons, and hope just out of reach.
The village burial grounds lie silent at the edge of the trees, where stones lean and stories sleep beneath the red soil.
The well is our gathering place, where the rope creaks, the pots ring, and the morning light dances on the water's surface.

- St. Martin de Porres -
The Broom of God's Joy
My dear friend, pull up a chair and settle in, for I've got a tale to spin that's equal parts laughter, tears of joy, and a whole lot of God's grace.
You see, life in Lima back in the late 1500s wasn't all sunshine and fiestas
Though we Peruvians do love our fiestas
But it was full of surprises, much like a piñata at a child's party.
I'm no grand storyteller like those bards in the old tales, just a humble mulatto lay brother who spent his days sweeping floors and tending to the sick.
But God, in His infinite humor, decided to make my life a bit of an adventure.
So, let me take you back to where it all began, with a chuckle or two along the way, because if you can't laugh at your own mishaps, what's the point of living?
I was born in 1579, right here in Lima, the city of kings, though I felt more like the court jester most days.
My father was Don Juan de Porres, a Spanish knight with a mustache that could sweep the streets and a heart that wandered a bit too freely.
My mother, Ana Velázquez, was a freed woman from Panama, as dark and beautiful as a moonless night, with a spirit fiercer than a condor's cry.
They weren't married, mind you
Oh, the scandals that caused!
But Don Juan acknowledged me and my little sister Juana as his own.
Still, he up and left us to fend for ourselves when I was just a wee lad, probably figuring a knight's life was too glamorous for diaper duty.
Ha!
Little did he know, God had bigger plans, and they involved more humility than a peacock could handle.
Growing up poor in Lima meant scraping by on whatever the good Lord provided, which wasn't always much more than a bowl of maize porridge and a prayer.
My mother worked her fingers to the bone as a laundress, and I learned early on that clean clothes and a clean conscience go hand in hand.
I was a scrawny thing, with my mother's dark skin and curly hair, which earned me no small share of sideways glances from the fine Spanish folk.
"Mulatto," they'd whisper, as if it were a curse.
But I?
I just smiled and kept sweeping.
You see, from the cradle, I had this funny notion that everyone
Rich or poor, light or dark
Was made in God's image.
Why fuss over colors when the rainbow's got them all?
At twelve, Mother apprenticed me to a barber-surgeon.
Now, that was an education!
Imagine a boy with steady hands but a heart softer than overripe mango learning to wield razors and lancets.
I'd trim beards, pull teeth, and mix poultices, all while the patients grumbled about the heat or their aching gums.
One day, a pompous merchant came in, demanding a shave so close he could kiss his own reflection.
I nicked him just a tad
Nothing serious, mind you
And he hollered like I'd stolen his soul!
"You clumsy half-breed!" he bellowed.
I bowed low, apologized profusely, and offered to tend the cut for free.
By the end, he was laughing …
Calling me his "little miracle worker." That's when I first felt that tug, that whisper from above: healing wasn't just about the body; it was about the soul.
And humor?
Well, let's just say I learned to laugh off the insults, turning them into prayers for the insulters.
God has a way of flipping the script, doesn't He?
Three years into my apprenticeship, at fifteen, I couldn't ignore the call any longer.
The Dominicans at the Convento de la Rosa
Ah, the Rosary Convent
Had captured my heart.
I'd sneak peeks during processions, watching those friars in their white habits, preaching fire and mercy.
One evening, after a particularly grueling day of stitching wounds …
I knelt before a crucifix and promised God: "If You'll have me, I'll serve You till my last breath." The next day, I applied to join the Third Order of St.
Dominic as a lay brother.
But oh, the hurdles!
Because of my mixed blood, some grumbled.
"A mulatto in our ranks?" they muttered.
The prior, though
Bless his kind soul
Saw past the skin and into the spirit.
He took me on as a "donado," a sort of helper without vows at first.
I swept floors, tended the garden, and washed dishes, all with a song in my heart.
It was like being invited to the King's banquet after years of begging scraps
Pure joy!
After some time, proving my mettle (and dodging a few suspicious stares), I was allowed to profess as a full lay brother in 1603.
No priesthood for me; I was content with the broom and the basin.
"Brother Martin," they'd say, "you're the heart of this house." And I?
I'd grin and reply, "No, sirs, I'm just the broom
God does the sweeping!" Life in the convent was a whirlwind of duties: barber, surgeon, infirmarian, almoner
You name it, I juggled it like a circus performer on market day.
But juggling came with its funny falls.
Take the time I was distributing alms to the poor at the gate.
Our daily bread ration was meager, but I couldn't bear seeing the hungry faces.
One widow with five little ones tugged at my habit, her eyes pleading.
"Brother, just a crust?" I slipped her an extra loaf, then another for good measure.
By noon, the kitchen was in uproar!
"Martin, where's the bread gone?" the procurator thundered.
I hung my head, mumbling, "To where it was needed, Father." He sighed, but later I found him slipping extras himself.
See?
God's humor
Turning a scolding into a lesson in charity.
My days were filled with the sick, both in the convent and out in Lima's bustling streets.
The city was a melting pot: Spaniards lording it over, indigenous folk toiling, Africans shipped in chains like cargo.
My heart ached for them all, but especially the slaves.
I'd sneak into the docks at night, bandaging wounds from the whips, whispering prayers for freedom.
One fellow, a giant named Diego, had a leg so infected it looked like overcooked yuca.
The surgeons had given up, but I wouldn't.
With herbs from the garden and a novena to St.
Dominic, I tended him day and night.
"You're mad, Martin," he'd chuckle through the pain.
"Mad for Christ," I'd wink back.
Miraculously, the leg healed, and Diego became my shadow, helping with chores until he bought his freedom.
We laughed about it later: "You saved my leg, Brother
I owe you a dance!" And dance we did, at a secret gathering, feet stomping to African drums under the stars.
God must've smiled at that joyful racket.
But oh, the animals!
Folks still tease me about my "zoo" at the convent.
Mice nibbling the grain stores?
Instead of traps, I'd gather them up gently, like wayward children, and relocate them to the fields.
"Brother Martin talks to rats!" the novices would snicker.
Once, a friar caught me feeding a stray dog scraps from my own meager meal.
"Even the beasts get your charity?" he huffed.
I replied, "Father, if God feeds the birds, why not this pup?" He rolled his eyes, but the next day, that same friar was sneaking bones to the dog himself.
And the cats
Mercy, the cats!
I ran a sort of hospice for them at my sister's house, bandaging paws and nursing kittens.
One tabby, I called her Whiskers, followed me everywhere, even into the chapel.
During Mass, she'd curl at my feet, purring so loud the priest paused mid-homily.
"Martin, your admirer disrupts the peace!" he'd whisper.
I'd blush and shush her, but inside, I laughed
Proof that God's love extends to every creature, furry or not.
Now, let's talk penances, because if charity is my left hand, penance is my right
And both got a workout!
I longed for the missions, to earn martyrdom in some far-off land.
But obedience kept me in Lima, so I turned my body into the battlefield.
I'd sleep on the floor with a log for a pillow, wear a hair shirt that itched like a thousand fleas, and fast until my stomach played tunes like a street musician.
The brothers worried: "Martin, you'll waste away!" I'd quip, "Better a thin soul in heaven than a fat one in purgatory!" But God, in His whimsical way …
Balanced it with gifts I never sought.
Bilocation, they called it
Me appearing in two places at once.
Once, during a storm, I was seen comforting a dying man in the countryside while scrubbing pots in the kitchen.
The friar who fetched me exclaimed, "But Brother, you were just there!" I shrugged: "God's legs are longer than mine." Aerial flights?
Ha!
I'd levitate in prayer, floating like a leaf on the wind.
The novices tried peeking once, only to tumble in fright.
"See?" I laughed later.

"Even angels need privacy!"
Friendships?
They were the spice in my stew of service.
St.
Rose of Lima
Dear Rosa, what a firecracker!
She was a Dominican tertiary like me, with eyes that pierced the soul and a temper hotter than chili peppers.
We'd meet in the garden, sharing stories of visions and woes.
Once, she was ill, refusing food in her austerities.
I brought her a simple broth, laced with a bit of humor: "Rosa, if you don't eat, how will you scold the devil properly?" She chuckled …
A rare sound from that mystic, and sipped it down.
We prayed together for Lima's poor, and oh, the laughs we'd share over the friars' quirks.
"That prior," she'd mimic, "thinks sweeping is beneath him!" I'd nod: "But God sweeps us all clean in the end." Then there was Blessed John Massias …
Another lay brother at a nearby priory.
We'd swap tales of alms-giving; he once multiplied loaves like our Lord, or so they said.
"Martin, your miracles are flashier," he'd tease.

"Nonsense," I'd retort, "yours feed the belly; mine just amuse the eyes!"
Lima's orphans tugged hardest at my heart.
I founded a refuge for them, a foundling hospital where tiny souls could find warmth.
Picture this: me, a grown man with a beard like a broom, cradling babes and singing lullabies in Spanish, Quechua, and bits of African tongue from the slaves.
One night, a basket arrived at the gate
Inside, twins, abandoned and wailing.
I rocked them till dawn, whispering, "God's got you now." The older brothers called it my "soft spot." Soft?
Perhaps.
But in a world of hard edges, softness is the real strength.
And humor kept us going: the twins grew into mischief-makers, one always stealing my rosary beads.
"Like father, like sons," I'd joke, though they weren't mine by blood.
As years rolled on, like waves on Callao's shore, my body began to falter.
Fevers came and went, but I pushed on, tending the infirmary even from my sickbed.
The superiors, bless them, tried to ease my load, but I'd wave them off: "If I stop serving, what good am I?" In 1639, on November 3, the end drew near.
The convent gathered, prelates and nobles mingling with the poor
Quite the crowd for a simple brother!
I received the Last Sacraments, my heart light as a feather.
"Thank You, Lord," I murmured, "for the laughter, the love, the lessons." As I slipped away, I glimpsed Heaven's gate, ajar with welcoming light.
No fanfare, just peace.
And now, from that eternal vantage, I look back with a warm chuckle.
My life?
A tapestry of mishaps and mercies, woven by hands far wiser than mine.
I wasn't a hero, just a fellow who tried to love as Christ loved
Extravagantly, inclusively, with a dash of joy.
You, my friend, carry that same call.
In your daily sweeps
Whether floors or worries
See the face of God in all.
Laugh at the stumbles, extend a hand to the fallen, and remember: even a mulatto broom can sweep souls to sanctity.
God's got a sense of humor, after all; why shouldn't we join in?
Ah, but I skipped ahead too quickly!
Let's linger on those early convent days, shall we?
When I first donned the habit, it hung loose on my frame, like a tent on a twig.
The novices ribbed me endlessly: "Brother Martin, did you borrow that from Father Elephant?" I'd retort with a bow, "Better loose than tight
Leaves room for the Holy Spirit!" Sweeping the cloisters became my meditation; each stroke a prayer for the world's woes.
One afternoon, as I pushed the broom, a superior caught me pausing to help a lame beggar at the wall.
"Martin, your duties!" he scolded.
I smiled: "Father, the dust waits; souls don't." He grumbled but let it pass, and soon enough …
Beggars lined up not just for alms, but for my silly stories to lift their spirits.
The infirmary was my true playground, though "play" meant wrestling fevers and despair.
During a plague scare in 1609, the city panicked
Folks barricading doors, friars chanting litanies.
I, fool that I was, ventured out, maskless and merry, anointing the afflicted.
"Brother, you'll catch your death!" a friar warned.
"If I do," I quipped, "at least I'll die serving, not cowering." I nursed dozens, from haughty hidalgos to forgotten slaves, all equal in God's eyes.
One old indigenous woman, bedridden and bitter …
Spat at my approach: "Go away, dark one!" I wiped my face, offered her water, and told her of my mother's Panamanian tales …
Stories of jaguars and stars.
By week's end, she gripped my hand: "Stay, hijo mio." Her soul mended before her body, and we shared laughs over her "tiger" temper.
Miracles?
They snuck up like playful puppies.
Take the multiplying food bit.
Our alms basket was bare one feast day, yet fifty poor waited.
I prayed over it, and lo
Loaves appeared aplenty!
The brothers gawked: "How?" I shrugged: "God hates empty stomachs more than I do." Or the time a friar fell from the roof, leg shattered.
Surgeons shook their heads, but I applied salves and faith.
He walked by dawn, dancing a jig: "Martin, you're a wizard!" "No, sir

Just God's apprentice."
With animals, the humor multiplied.
Rats in the refectory?
I'd preach to them: "Little brothers, the crumbs are for men; find your supper elsewhere!" Witnesses swore the rodents listened, scampering off in orderly file.
A friar tested it once, hiding cheese to lure them back.
Come midnight, not a nibble.
"Your sermon worked too well!" he laughed.
And the birds
Sparrows nesting in the rafters, chirping during silent prayer.
I'd shoo them gently, only for them to return, perching on my shoulder.
"See?
Even they know you're holy," a novice teased.
Holy?
Me?

I preferred "handy with a broom."
My sister Juana's home became extension of the convent
A haven for strays, human and otherwise.
She'd roll her eyes at my "guests": "Martin, this cat or that orphan
Which next?" I'd hug her: "Both, mi hermana
God's family is big!" We raised her daughter there too, after Juana's husband passed.
The girl called me "Tío Sweepy," and we'd chase chickens in the yard, giggling till our sides ached.
Friendships deepened over decades.
With Rose, we'd debate visions: hers fiery, mine gentle.
"You float like a cloud, Martin," she'd say.
"And you burn like the sun, Rosa!" Blessed John and I raced alms routes, betting who fed more.
"Loser sweeps the winner's cell!" I'd win by a hair, then sweep anyway
Obedience, you know.
As age crept in, ailments nipped: rheumatism in my joints, like rusty hinges.
Still, I rose at dawn, broom in hand.
The end came softly, surrounded by song.
From Heaven, I watch you now
Live warmly, love wholesomely, laugh heartily.
That's the Porres way!
Let's delve deeper into a particular escapade, one that still makes the angels chuckle.
It was around 1620, during a harsh rainy season.
The convent roof leaked like a sieve, and debts piled higher than the Andes.
The procurator, a fretful sort named Brother Tomas, paced the chapter room: "We're ruined!
Creditors at the gate!" I, overhearing, stepped in: "Father, take me instead.
I'm Order property
Sell this old mulatto to pay the bill!" The room erupted in laughter, even Tomas guffawing: "Martin …
You'd fetch two pesos and a smile!" The crisis eased when a donor appeared, but the tale spread, turning my blunder into legend.
Humility with humor
God's perfect recipe.
Another time, tending a nobleman's son with fever, the boy delirious, calling for sweets.
The family despaired, but I fetched honeyed figs from the kitchen (pilfered with a wink).
"Miracle food!" the lad exclaimed upon recovery.
The father, Don Balthasar, insisted on "adopting" me as son.
"Why a mulatto father?" I protested.
"Better a saintly one than a stuffy Spaniard!" he boomed.
We became fast friends, him funding my orphanages, me praying for his soul.
The slaves' plight fueled my fire.
I'd teach them catechism in hidden groves, their chants blending African rhythms with Dominican plainsong.
One, a woman named Maria, bore lashes from her master.
I confronted him
Me, a lowly brother!
With gentle words: "Sir, Christ's back bore more for her sake." He softened, freeing her.
"Your tongue's sharper than any whip," he admitted.
Laughter followed tears, as Maria danced her thanks.
In quiet moments, I'd reflect on my parents.
Mother died in peace, Father reconciled at last, confessing on his deathbed.
"Son," he whispered, "forgive my wanderings." "All forgiven, Papa
God's the true Father." Wholesome closure, with a humorous twist: he left me his old sword, which I melted for alms pots!
As 1639 dawned, visions intensified
Saints welcoming me home.
The brothers noticed my glow: "Martin, you're shining!" "Just polished by prayer," I'd jest.
On All Souls' Eve, I lay down, heart full.
"Adios, dear ones

See you in eternity!"
From above, my story's simple: love without limits, serve with smiles, find God in the ordinary.
You can too
Start with a kind word, a shared laugh.
That's sainthood, warm and wholesome as a Lima sunrise.
